Medicine-03.question: ১) Sputum of pulmonary oedema isn’t
Medicine-03.exp:
In acute pulmonary oedema, fluid leaks from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli due to increased hydrostatic pressure (most commonly from left ventricular failure).

The characteristic sputum is:

  • Serous – because it is mainly transudative fluid.

  • Frothy – due to mixing of oedema fluid with air.

  • Pink – because a small amount of red blood cells may leak into the alveoli, producing the classic pink frothy sputum.

Mucopurulent sputum indicates the presence of pus (neutrophils) and is typically seen in respiratory infections such as bronchitis, bronchiectasis, lung abscess, or pneumonia, not pulmonary oedema.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • ক) Serous – ✔ Characteristic of pulmonary oedema.

  • খ) Frothy – ✔ Classic finding due to air mixed with oedema fluid.

  • গ) Pink – ✔ Pink frothy sputum is a hallmark of acute pulmonary oedema.

  • ঘ) Mucopurulent –  Suggests infection rather than pulmonary oedema.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Feature Pulmonary Oedema
Typical sputum Pink, frothy, serous
Common cause Left ventricular failure
Breath sound Fine bibasal crackles
Chest X-ray Bat-wing (perihilar) shadowing, Kerley B lines
Emergency treatment Oxygen, diuretics (e.g., furosemide), nitrates (when appropriate), treat underlying cause

Exam Pearl

"Pink frothy sputum = Acute pulmonary oedema."
Mucopurulent sputum = Respiratory infection (e.g., pneumonia/bronchiectasis), not pulmonary oedema.

Medicine-03.question: ২) Most common extra pulmonary site of TB
Medicine-03.exp: The most common extrapulmonary site of tuberculosis (TB) is the lymph node, particularly the cervical lymph nodes (tuberculous lymphadenitis or scrofula). Extrapulmonary TB results from lymphohematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals. Patients typically present with painless, slowly enlarging lymph nodes that may become matted and develop sinus tracts. Bone TB (especially spinal TB or Pott disease), gastrointestinal TB (commonly involving the ileocecal region), and CNS TB (e.g., tuberculous meningitis) are well-recognized extrapulmonary manifestations but occur less frequently than lymph node involvement. Therefore, lymph node is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩) The majority of pulmonary emboli arise from propagation of
Medicine-03.exp: The majority of pulmonary emboli (PE) arise from propagation or embolization of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), most commonly originating in the deep veins of the lower limbs (especially the femoral and iliac veins) or pelvis. A thrombus dislodges, travels through the venous circulation, passes the right side of the heart, and lodges in the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary embolism. Varicose veins are superficial veins and rarely cause clinically significant PE. Fractures, particularly long-bone fractures, and blunt trauma increase the risk of DVT and subsequent PE but are not the direct source of most pulmonary emboli. Therefore, DVT is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৪) Whispering pectoriloquy is a feature of
Medicine-03.exp: Whispering pectoriloquy is an auscultatory sign of lung consolidation, classically seen in pneumonia. Normally, whispered sounds are muffled as they pass through air-filled alveoli. In consolidation, the alveoli are filled with inflammatory exudate, which conducts high-frequency sound more efficiently. As a result, whispered words are heard clearly and distinctly over the affected area. Other signs of consolidation include bronchial breath sounds, bronchophony, egophony, and increased vocal resonance. In contrast, pneumothorax and pleural effusion reduce sound transmission, leading to diminished or absent breath sounds and decreased vocal resonance. Collapse (atelectasis) may produce variable findings depending on whether the bronchus is patent, but whispering pectoriloquy is classically associated with pneumonia.

Medicine-03.question: ৫) In pott’s disease there is involvement of
Medicine-03.exp: Pott’s disease refers to tuberculosis of the spine, the most common form of skeletal (bone) tuberculosis. It usually affects the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, leading to destruction of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs. Patients typically present with chronic back pain, localized tenderness, kyphotic deformity (gibbus), and, in advanced cases, neurological deficits due to spinal cord compression. Paravertebral or psoas abscesses may also develop. Lymph node TB, gastrointestinal TB, and CNS TB are important extrapulmonary forms of tuberculosis but are distinct from Pott’s disease. Therefore, bone is the correct answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৬) Absent breath sound with hyper resonant percussion note indicates
Medicine-03.exp: Pneumothorax classically presents with absent or markedly diminished breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note over the affected hemithorax due to the presence of air in the pleural space. The trapped air separates the lung from the chest wall, preventing normal transmission of breath sounds and producing hyper-resonance on percussion. Patients typically present with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Pneumonia causes bronchial breath sounds with a dull percussion note due to consolidation. Collapse (atelectasis) usually produces reduced breath sounds with a dull percussion note. Pleural effusion also causes absent or reduced breath sounds, but percussion is stony dull, not hyper-resonant. Therefore, pneumothorax is the best answer

Medicine-03.question: ৭) Definitive diagnosis of TB requires
Medicine-03.exp: Mycobacterial culture is the definitive (gold standard) method for diagnosing tuberculosis (TB) because it confirms the presence of viable Mycobacterium tuberculosis and allows drug susceptibility testing. Although culture is highly sensitive and specific, it requires several weeks for results. GeneXpert (CBNAAT) is a rapid molecular test that detects M. tuberculosis DNA and rifampicin resistance within hours, making it an excellent initial diagnostic test, but it is not the definitive gold standard. Sputum cytology has no role in diagnosing TB, and the Mantoux test (MT) indicates prior sensitization to TB antigens but cannot distinguish latent from active disease. Therefore, culture is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৮) Stony dull percussion note
Medicine-03.exp: A stony dull percussion note is the classical physical sign of pleural effusion, where fluid accumulates in the pleural space. The fluid markedly dampens percussion vibrations, producing an extremely dull ("stony dull") note. Other examination findings include reduced or absent breath sounds, decreased vocal fremitus, and reduced vocal resonance over the effusion. In contrast, pneumonia and lung collapse (atelectasis) usually produce a dull percussion note rather than stony dullness, while pneumothorax produces a hyper-resonant percussion note because of air in the pleural cavity. Therefore, pleural effusion is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৯) First line diagnostic test in pulmonary embolism?
Medicine-03.exp: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the first-line diagnostic imaging test for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) in hemodynamically stable patients. It directly visualizes thrombi within the pulmonary arteries and has high sensitivity and specificity. CTPA has largely replaced conventional pulmonary angiography because it is rapid, widely available, and can identify alternative causes of chest symptoms. Duplex ultrasonography is useful for detecting deep vein thrombosis (DVT) but does not diagnose PE directly. MRA is not routinely used because of limited availability and lower diagnostic accuracy. CTA is a general term; the specific investigation for PE is CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA). Therefore, CTPA is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১০) Gout is an adverse effect of
Medicine-03.exp: Pyrazinamide commonly causes hyperuricaemia by reducing renal excretion of uric acid, which may precipitate acute gouty arthritis. Although asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is more common than clinical gout, pyrazinamide is the anti-tubercular drug classically associated with this adverse effect. Ethambutol can also increase serum uric acid and occasionally contribute to gout, making the question somewhat ambiguous. However, in standard medical examinations, pyrazinamide is regarded as the single best answer because it has the strongest association with clinically significant hyperuricaemia and gout. Isoniazid is mainly associated with peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, while streptomycin is associated with ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

Medicine-03.question: ১১) CURB-65 scoring system measures severity of
Medicine-03.exp:
CURB-65 is a clinical scoring system used to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and to guide decisions regarding hospitalization and prognosis. The score assigns one point each for:

  • Confusion

  • Blood Urea > 7 mmol/L

  • Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min

  • Low Blood pressure (SBP < 90 mmHg or DBP ≤ 60 mmHg)

  • Age 65 years or older

Higher scores are associated with increased mortality and the need for inpatient management. Asthma, COPD, and bronchiectasis have their own severity assessment tools and are not evaluated using CURB-65. Therefore, pneumonia is the correct answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১২) Blood-stained pleural fluid isn’t found in
Medicine-03.exp: Blood-stained pleural fluid is commonly seen in malignancy, pulmonary infarction due to pulmonary embolism, and may also occur in acute pancreatitis, where inflammation and enzyme leakage can produce a hemorrhagic pleural effusion. In contrast, pleural effusion due to cardiac failure is typically a clear, straw-colored transudate resulting from increased hydrostatic pressure and is not blood stained. Therefore, among the given options, cardiac failure is the condition in which blood-stained pleural fluid is generally not found, making it the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৩) Most common infecting agent in CAP
Medicine-03.exp: The most common causative organism of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). It is responsible for the largest proportion of bacterial CAP cases across all age groups. Patients typically present with acute fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and lobar consolidation on chest imaging. Staphylococcus aureus is a less common cause and is often associated with post-influenza pneumonia or hospital-acquired infection. Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia, especially in younger adults, while Legionella pneumophila causes severe atypical pneumonia and is associated with contaminated water sources. Therefore, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৪) Cause of type-2 respiratory failure
Medicine-03.exp: Type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is characterized by PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg with hypoxaemia due to alveolar hypoventilation. The most common cause is an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), where airflow obstruction and reduced alveolar ventilation lead to carbon dioxide retention. Acute asthma can also cause type II respiratory failure in severe, life-threatening attacks, but it is less common than COPD. Pneumonia and ARDS usually produce Type I (hypoxaemic) respiratory failure, characterized by low PaO₂ with normal or low PaCO₂ in the early stages. Therefore, COPD is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৫) Type of hypersensitivity reaction in TB
Medicine-03.exp: Tuberculosis (TB) is characterized by a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction, which is cell-mediated rather than antibody-mediated. After infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sensitized T lymphocytes (Th1 cells) release cytokines such as interferon-γ (IFN-γ), activating macrophages and leading to granuloma formation with caseous necrosis. This immune response is responsible for the positive Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test, which develops 48–72 hours after antigen exposure. Anaphylactic (Type I), immune complex-mediated (Type III), and complement-based mechanisms are not the primary hypersensitivity reactions involved in TB. Therefore, delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity is the correct answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৬) Regular preventer therapy of asthma
Medicine-03.exp: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of regular preventer therapy for asthma because they suppress chronic airway inflammation, reduce airway hyperresponsiveness, decrease exacerbations, and improve symptom control and lung function. They are recommended as the first-line controller medication for patients requiring regular preventive treatment. Inhaled LABAs should not be used as monotherapy in asthma because they increase the risk of severe exacerbations unless combined with an ICS. LAMAs are add-on therapy for selected patients with persistent symptoms despite ICS-LABA treatment. Leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) are alternative or add-on controller medications but are generally less effective than low-dose ICS. Therefore, low-dose ICS is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৭) Which anti-TB drug forms the cornerstone of 6-mlnths chemotherapy
Medicine-03.exp: Rifampicin is the cornerstone of the standard 6-month chemotherapy regimen for drug-sensitive tuberculosis because of its potent sterilizing activity against both rapidly multiplying and slowly replicating Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The inclusion of rifampicin throughout the treatment course allows the regimen to be shortened from 9–18 months to 6 months. Standard therapy consists of 2 months of HRZE (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) followed by 4 months of HR (Isoniazid and Rifampicin). Although isoniazid is highly bactericidal and an essential first-line drug, rifampicin is the key drug that makes the 6-month short-course regimen possible. Pyrazinamide mainly shortens the intensive phase, while ethambutol primarily helps prevent the emergence of resistance.

Medicine-03.question: ১৮) Feature of acute severe asthma
Medicine-03.option3: Inability to complete sentence in 1 breath
Medicine-03.exp: Inability to complete a sentence in one breath is a classic clinical feature of acute severe asthma and reflects significant airflow obstruction and respiratory distress. It is included among the bedside indicators of severe asthma, along with respiratory rate ≥25/min, heart rate ≥110/min, and PEF 33–50% of predicted or best. Coma and hypotension are features of life-threatening or near-fatal asthma, not acute severe asthma. Delirium is also a sign of severe hypoxaemia or impending respiratory failure rather than uncomplicated acute severe asthma. Therefore, the inability to complete a sentence in one breath is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ১৯) Retrobulbar neuritis is a major adverse reaction observed in therapy with
Medicine-03.exp: Ethambutol is classically associated with retrobulbar optic neuritis (optic neuropathy), a dose-related adverse effect characterized by decreased visual acuity, central scotoma, and impaired red-green color vision. The toxicity is usually reversible if the drug is discontinued promptly but may become permanent if unrecognized. Patients receiving ethambutol should have baseline and periodic assessment of visual acuity and color vision, especially with prolonged therapy or higher doses. Isoniazid commonly causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, pyrazinamide is associated with hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia, and streptomycin causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Therefore, ethambutol is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২০) Indication for assisted ventilation in acute severe asthma excludes
Medicine-03.exp: The question is somewhat ambiguous, as hypotension may occur in life-threatening asthma and can accompany impending respiratory arrest. However, accepted indications for assisted (mechanical) ventilation in acute severe asthma include exhaustion, drowsiness or reduced level of consciousness, worsening or persistent hypercapnia, respiratory arrest, and severe hypoxaemia despite optimal treatment. Delirium may also indicate severe hypoxaemia or hypercapnia and is considered a sign of impending respiratory failure. Hypotension alone is not a standard direct indication for assisted ventilation; it should prompt evaluation for causes such as tension pneumothorax, dynamic hyperinflation, or shock. Therefore, hypotension is the best answer to the "excludes" question.

Medicine-03.question: ২১) Investigation of choice in Bronchiectasis
Medicine-03.exp: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is the investigation of choice and the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosing bronchiectasis. HRCT clearly demonstrates the characteristic features, including irreversible bronchial dilatation, bronchial wall thickening, lack of normal bronchial tapering, and bronchi visible close to the pleural surface. It also helps determine the extent and distribution of disease, which is important for management. Chest X-ray (CXR) may show suggestive changes such as tram-track opacities or ring shadows but has limited sensitivity and can be normal in early disease. MRI and ultrasonography (USG) are not routinely used for diagnosing bronchiectasis. Therefore, HRCT is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২২) Straw colored pleural fluid indicates
Medicine-03.exp: Straw-colored pleural fluid is classically seen in congestive cardiac failure (CCF), where the pleural effusion is a transudate caused by increased hydrostatic pressure. The fluid is typically clear, pale yellow (straw-colored), and has low protein and low lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). In contrast, pleural effusions due to tuberculosis (TB), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are usually exudative, with higher protein and inflammatory cell content. TB effusions are often straw-colored as well, making the question somewhat ambiguous. However, in standard examination practice, the classic association of a simple straw-colored transudative pleural effusion is CCF, making it the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৩) Commonest cause of recurrent pleural effusion?
Medicine-03.exp: Bronchial carcinoma is the commonest cause of recurrent pleural effusion, particularly in older adults. Malignant pleural effusions tend to recur because of persistent pleural involvement, impaired lymphatic drainage, and ongoing tumor activity. Patients often require repeated thoracentesis, pleurodesis, or an indwelling pleural catheter for symptom control. Pneumonia usually causes a parapneumonic effusion that resolves with appropriate antibiotic treatment. Tuberculosis can produce pleural effusion, but with effective anti-tubercular therapy, recurrence is uncommon. Lymphoma may also cause recurrent malignant pleural effusions but is less common than bronchogenic (bronchial) carcinoma. Therefore, bronchial carcinoma is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৪) X-ray chest shows cavity with air–fluid level
Medicine-03.exp: A lung abscess classically appears on chest X-ray as a thick-walled cavity containing an air–fluid level. It results from necrosis of lung parenchyma, usually following aspiration of oropharyngeal contents or severe bacterial pneumonia. Patients typically present with fever, productive cough, foul-smelling sputum, and constitutional symptoms. Pneumonia usually shows consolidation without a cavitary air–fluid level unless complicated by abscess formation. Bronchiectasis is characterized by dilated bronchi with tram-track or ring shadows on imaging rather than a single thick-walled cavity. Lung cancer may cavitate, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, but an air–fluid level is less typical and usually suggests secondary infection. Therefore, lung abscess is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৫) Removal of more than 1.5 L of pleural fluid at a time may risk
Medicine-03.exp: Removal of more than 1.5 L of pleural fluid during a single thoracentesis increases the risk of re-expansion pulmonary edema (re-expansion pulmonary injury). This uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication occurs when a chronically collapsed lung re-expands rapidly, leading to increased pulmonary capillary permeability and edema. Patients may develop cough, chest pain, dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, and new pulmonary infiltrates after the procedure. To minimize this risk, many guidelines recommend limiting initial fluid removal to 1–1.5 L, particularly if pleural pressure is not being monitored. Pneumothorax is a procedural complication of thoracentesis but is not specifically related to removing a large volume. Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale are not complications of large-volume pleural fluid drainage. Therefore, re-expansion pulmonary injury is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৬) D-shaped shadow in CXR indicates
Medicine-03.exp: A D-shaped (lentiform) opacity on chest X-ray is characteristic of empyema, which is a collection of pus in the pleural space. Because the infected fluid is often loculated by fibrinous adhesions, it forms a biconvex or D-shaped pleural-based shadow with obtuse angles against the chest wall rather than freely layering. Patients typically present with fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, and features of sepsis. Pleural effusion usually produces a meniscus sign with blunting of the costophrenic angle rather than a D-shaped opacity. Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura and often has no characteristic radiographic shadow, while pneumothorax shows a pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings and hyperlucency. Therefore, empyema is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৭) Which one is central to the management of breathlessness in COPD?
Medicine-03.exp: Pulmonary rehabilitation is central to the long-term management of breathlessness in COPD. It combines supervised exercise training, education, breathing techniques, nutritional advice, and psychological support, leading to improved exercise tolerance, reduced dyspnoea, enhanced quality of life, and fewer hospital admissions. Although bronchodilators are the cornerstone of pharmacological treatment and help relieve airflow limitation, pulmonary rehabilitation provides the greatest sustained improvement in functional breathlessness. Oxygen therapy is indicated only for patients with chronic severe hypoxaemia and does not relieve breathlessness in non-hypoxaemic patients. Inhaled corticosteroids are reserved for selected patients with frequent exacerbations and are not the primary treatment for dyspnoea. Therefore, pulmonary rehabilitation is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৮) COPD is diagnosed when post bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV/FVC is less than
Medicine-03.exp: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is diagnosed when post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrates a FEV₁/FVC ratio < 0.70 (70%), indicating persistent airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. Spirometry should be performed after administration of an inhaled bronchodilator to distinguish COPD from reversible airflow obstruction, such as asthma. Once the diagnosis is established, the severity of airflow limitation is graded according to the post-bronchodilator FEV₁ (% predicted). A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio confirms airflow obstruction, while the FEV₁ value determines its severity. Ratios of 30%, 40%, or 50% are far below the diagnostic threshold and do not define COPD. Therefore, FEV₁/FVC <70% is the correct answer.

Medicine-03.question: ২৯) Most common cause of bronchiectasis
Medicine-03.exp: The question is context-dependent. Worldwide, post-infectious (suppurative) pneumonia remains the most common acquired cause of bronchiectasis, especially in regions where severe respiratory infections are common. Recurrent or severe bacterial pneumonia causes destruction of the bronchial wall, resulting in irreversible bronchial dilatation. Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of bronchiectasis in children and in many Western countries, but it is not the most common cause overall in many developing countries or adult populations. Tuberculosis is an important post-infectious cause but is less common than suppurative pneumonia overall. Bronchial tumors may cause localized bronchiectasis due to obstruction but are an uncommon cause.

Medicine-03.question: ৩০) Symptoms of asthma worsens in the
Medicine-03.exp: Asthma symptoms typically worsen in the early morning hours (usually between 3–6 AM) because of circadian variation in airway function. During this time, endogenous cortisol and catecholamine levels are lowest, while vagal tone increases, leading to enhanced bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation. As a result, patients commonly experience wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and breathlessness on waking. Nocturnal or early morning symptoms are a hallmark of poorly controlled asthma and are included in assessing asthma control. Although symptoms may also occur at night, early morning worsening is the classic and most characteristic pattern.

Medicine-03.question: ৩১) Most common URTI
Medicine-03.exp: Acute coryza (the common cold) is the most common upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). It is usually caused by rhinoviruses, although coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and other respiratory viruses can also be responsible. Patients typically present with rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, and low-grade fever, and the illness is usually self-limiting. Acute pharyngitis and acute tonsillitis are also common URTIs but occur less frequently than the common cold. Bronchiolitis is a lower respiratory tract infection, primarily affecting infants, and is therefore not classified as a URTI. Hence, acute coryza is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩২) Which drug is added in initial add-on therapy step of management of asthma?
Medicine-03.exp: In the stepwise management of asthma, if symptoms remain uncontrolled on low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), the initial add-on therapy is an inhaled long-acting β₂-agonist (LABA). LABAs improve bronchodilation, reduce symptoms, enhance lung function, and decrease exacerbations. They must always be used in combination with an ICS and should never be prescribed as monotherapy in asthma because of the increased risk of severe exacerbations. LTRA (leukotriene receptor antagonist) is an alternative or additional controller when LABA is unsuitable or ineffective. LAMA is reserved as an add-on treatment for patients with persistent symptoms despite ICS-LABA therapy. Therefore, inhaled LABA is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৩) URTI are mostly
Medicine-03.exp: Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are predominantly viral in origin. Common causative viruses include rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, adenoviruses, influenza viruses, parainfluenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). These infections are usually self-limiting and are managed with supportive care rather than antibiotics. Bacterial URTIs, such as streptococcal pharyngitis, account for only a minority of cases and require specific antimicrobial therapy when confirmed or strongly suspected. Fungal and parasitic infections of the upper respiratory tract are rare and usually occur in immunocompromised individuals. Therefore, viral infections are the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৪) Feature suggesting near-fatal asthma
Medicine-03.exp: Raised PaCO₂ (hypercapnia) is a key feature of near-fatal asthma and indicates impending or established ventilatory failure due to severe airflow obstruction and respiratory muscle fatigue. In acute asthma, patients initially hyperventilate, resulting in a low PaCO₂. Therefore, a normal or elevated PaCO₂ is an ominous sign that warrants urgent intensive care assessment and consideration of mechanical ventilation. Silent chest, cyanosis, and exhaustion are also features of life-threatening asthma. However, near-fatal asthma is specifically defined by raised PaCO₂ and/or the need for mechanical ventilation. Hence, raised PaCO₂ is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৫) Lupus pernio is a presentation of
Medicine-03.exp: Lupus pernio is a characteristic chronic cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis. It presents as violaceous, indurated plaques or nodules over the nose, cheeks, lips, and ears and is strongly associated with chronic systemic sarcoidosis, particularly pulmonary involvement. Its presence often indicates more severe disease with upper respiratory tract and lung involvement. Histologically, it is characterized by non-caseating granulomas, the hallmark of sarcoidosis. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cystic fibrosis, and lung cancer are not associated with lupus pernio. Therefore, sarcoidosis is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৬) Feature of Macleod’s syndrome
Medicine-03.exp: Macleod syndrome (Swyer–James–Macleod syndrome) is characterized by unilateral hyperlucent lung (unilateral emphysema) due to post-infectious bronchiolitis obliterans, usually following a severe childhood respiratory infection. The affected lung is small, hyperinflated, and has reduced pulmonary vascular markings because of decreased perfusion. Patients may present with recurrent respiratory infections, chronic cough, exertional dyspnoea, or may remain asymptomatic. Chest X-ray shows a unilateral hyperlucent lung, and HRCT demonstrates air trapping and bronchiectatic changes. Bilateral emphysema, acute bronchitis, and chronic bronchitis are not characteristic features of Macleod syndrome. Therefore, unilateral emphysema is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৭) Cause of exudative pleural effusion
Medicine-03.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) commonly causes an exudative pleural effusion due to pleural inflammation (pleuritis). Exudative effusions result from increased capillary permeability caused by inflammation, infection, or malignancy and are characterized by high protein and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels (meeting Light's criteria). In contrast, congestive cardiac failure (CCF), nephrotic syndrome, and cirrhosis of the liver typically produce transudative pleural effusions due to increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased plasma oncotic pressure, without primary pleural inflammation. Therefore, SLE is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৮) Acute coryza is mostly caused by
Medicine-03.exp: Rhinovirus is the most common cause of acute coryza (common cold), accounting for approximately 30–50% of all cases. It is transmitted by respiratory droplets and direct contact, with symptoms including rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, and cough. The illness is usually self-limiting and resolves within 7–10 days. Coronaviruses are also common causes of the common cold but are less frequent than rhinoviruses. Adenoviruses can cause pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and respiratory infections, while respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) predominantly causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children. Therefore, rhinovirus is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৯) Antimicrobials causing pulmonary eosinophilia except
Medicine-03.exp: Drug-induced pulmonary eosinophilia is a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, cough, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates, and peripheral eosinophilia. Among antimicrobials, nitrofurantoin is the classic cause and is a well-recognized cause of both acute and chronic pulmonary toxicity. Penicillins and tetracyclines have also been reported to cause pulmonary eosinophilia, although much less commonly. Erythromycin is not classically associated with pulmonary eosinophilia and is therefore the best answer to the "except" question.

Medicine-03.question: ৪০) Most common manifestation of past asbestosis exposure
Medicine-03.exp: Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation of previous asbestos exposure. They are localized areas of hyalinized fibrous thickening involving the parietal pleura, commonly affecting the diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall. Pleural plaques are usually asymptomatic, often discovered incidentally on chest X-ray or CT scan, and serve as a marker of prior asbestos exposure rather than causing significant respiratory impairment. Diffuse parenchymal lung disease (asbestosis) develops after heavy, prolonged exposure and is less common than pleural plaques. Mesothelioma is a serious but much rarer malignancy associated with asbestos, while pleurisy is not the typical or most common manifestation of asbestos exposure. Therefore, pleural plaque is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৪১) Which investigation is done to detect the marker of severity in CAP
Medicine-03.exp: Full blood count (FBC) is performed in patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) to assess markers of disease severity. Leukocytosis or leukopenia may indicate severe infection, while thrombocytopenia can also suggest severe sepsis and a poorer prognosis. FBC is part of the routine laboratory evaluation alongside urea (used in the CURB-65 score), CRP, and other investigations. Blood culture helps identify the causative organism in severe CAP but is not a marker of severity. Sputum cytology has no role in assessing CAP severity. Chest X-ray (CXR) confirms the diagnosis and extent of pneumonia but is not used as a laboratory marker of severity.

Medicine-03.question: ৪২) Causes of chronic type-2 respiratory failure excludes
Medicine-03.exp: Chronic Type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is characterized by persistent hypoxaemia with elevated PaCO₂ due to chronic alveolar hypoventilation. Common causes include COPD, obstructive sleep apnea/obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and neuromuscular disorders (myopathies), all of which impair ventilation and lead to chronic carbon dioxide retention. In contrast, lobar collapse (atelectasis) is usually an acute localized pulmonary condition that primarily causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia (Type I respiratory failure). It is not a typical cause of chronic Type II respiratory failure. Therefore, lobar collapse is the single best answer to the "excludes" question.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৩) Most common complication of pneumonia
Medicine-03.exp: Parapneumonic pleural effusion is the most common complication of pneumonia. It develops when inflammation from the infected lung extends to the pleural space, leading to the accumulation of sterile or infected pleural fluid. Most parapneumonic effusions are uncomplicated and resolve with appropriate antibiotic therapy, although some may progress to empyema, which requires drainage. Empyema is a less common but more serious complication. ARDS occurs in severe pneumonia but is relatively uncommon. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) may occur in hospitalized patients because of immobility but is not a direct complication of pneumonia. Therefore, parapneumonic effusion is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৪) Most common cell type of lung cancer
Medicine-03.exp:
Adenocarcinoma is the most common histological type of lung cancer overall and has surpassed squamous cell carcinoma in incidence worldwide. It is the predominant subtype in non-smokers, women, and younger patients, although it also occurs in smokers. Adenocarcinoma typically arises in the peripheral lung and is the most common type associated with EGFR mutations and ALK rearrangements. Squamous cell carcinoma is strongly associated with smoking and usually arises centrally. Small-cell lung carcinoma is an aggressive neuroendocrine tumor, also strongly linked to smoking, while large-cell carcinoma is relatively uncommon.

Exam note: Older examination questions may list squamous cell carcinoma as the most common type. However, according to current standard medical teaching, the overall most common histological type is adenocarcinoma.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৫) Non metastatic extra pulmonary effect that is usually associated with small-cell lung cancer
Medicine-03.exp: Small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is strongly associated with paraneoplastic (non-metastatic) syndromes, the most common endocrine manifestation being syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) due to ectopic production of ADH. This results in hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine. Another classic paraneoplastic syndrome of SCLC is ectopic ACTH production causing Cushing syndrome. Hypercalcaemia is more commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma due to secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP). Carcinoid syndrome is associated with neuroendocrine carcinoid tumors rather than SCLC, and gynaecomastia is an uncommon paraneoplastic manifestation seen with hCG-producing tumors.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৬) The most frequent symptom of respiratory disease
Medicine-03.exp: Cough is the most frequent symptom of respiratory disease and is a protective reflex that helps clear secretions, foreign bodies, and irritants from the airways. It is a common presenting symptom in conditions such as upper respiratory tract infections, asthma, COPD, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, and lung cancer. Breathlessness (dyspnoea) is also a common respiratory symptom but is less frequent than cough as an initial presentation. Chest pain is usually associated with pleural or chest wall involvement, while haemoptysis is a relatively uncommon symptom that suggests more serious underlying pathology such as tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, or malignancy.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৭) Which disease occurs less frequently in smokers
Medicine-03.exp: Sarcoidosis occurs less frequently in smokers than in non-smokers. Although the exact mechanism is unclear, cigarette smoking appears to have a protective association against the development of sarcoidosis, possibly by altering immune responses and granuloma formation. In contrast, smoking is the strongest risk factor for COPD, markedly increases the risk of lung cancer, and is a major modifiable risk factor for myocardial infarction (MI) through its effects on atherosclerosis and thrombosis. Thus, among the options, sarcoidosis is the disease that is seen less commonly in smokers.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৮) Blood borne dissemination gives rise to
Medicine-03.exp: Blood-borne (haematogenous) dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis results in miliary tuberculosis. In this condition, tubercle bacilli spread through the bloodstream from a primary or reactivated focus and produce numerous tiny granulomatous lesions in multiple organs, including the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and meninges. Chest X-ray classically shows a diffuse miliary pattern of small, uniformly distributed nodules. Primary pulmonary TB usually represents the initial infection with a localized lung lesion (Ghon focus). Post-primary TB occurs due to reactivation of latent infection, commonly affecting the upper lobes. Secondary TB is a broader term for reactivation disease and is not specifically due to blood-borne dissemination.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৯) Which is the most symptom of lung cancer?
Medicine-03.exp: Cough is the most common symptom of lung cancer and is often the initial presenting complaint. It may occur due to irritation or obstruction of the bronchial tree by the tumor. A change in a chronic smoker’s cough pattern is an important warning sign. Other common symptoms include haemoptysis, dyspnoea, chest pain, weight loss, and fatigue, but they occur less frequently as presenting symptoms. Weight loss and malaise are usually features of advanced disease, while haemoptysis is an important but less common symptom. Therefore, cough is the single best answer.

Medicine-03.question: ৫০) Bilateral, predominantly basal & peripheral reticular opacities accompanied by honeycombing in HRCT indicates
Medicine-03.exp: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is classically characterized on high-resolution CT (HRCT) by bilateral, predominantly basal and peripheral reticular opacities with honeycombing, representing a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. Honeycombing reflects end-stage fibrotic destruction of lung architecture with formation of cystic air spaces. Patients typically present with progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, and restrictive lung function impairment. Sarcoidosis usually shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and upper lobe predominant fibrosis. Cystic fibrosis causes bronchiectasis, mucus plugging, and recurrent infections rather than a UIP pattern. Lung cancer does not produce this diffuse basal peripheral honeycombing pattern.
